extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim limitations render a claim patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 by providing 'significantly more' than a judicial exception (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas). Focuses on when additional elements are mere instructions to 'apply it', insignificant extra-solution activity, and field-of-use/technological-environment limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must explain when claim limitations are mere 'apply it' instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that do not amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent), such as mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If limitations merely instruct application of an exception (e.g., implementing on a generic computer), explain why they are not meaningful limitations; see Alice and MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating subject matter eligibility rejections. Provide claim-specific reasoning showing lack of meaningful limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Result-oriented, functional claiming that covers any solution with no mechanism is equivalent to saying 'apply it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-focused claims that lack steps or details of how the computer performed modifications (or how the result is achieved) are likely not 'significantly more' (cites Electric Power Group, Intellectual Ventures, Internet Patents Corp.). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or way to achieve an outcome may provide significantly more. Use case examples (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One) to explain why lack of implementation detail fails eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim invokes a computer or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (use of general-purpose computers in their ordinary capacity does not add significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a computer to receive, store, or transmit data, or adding generic computer components to an abstract idea, is insufficient (cites Affinity Labs, TLI Communications, Alice). Claims that improve computer capabilities or existing technology (Enfish, McRO) may provide significantly more. Provide claim-specific analysis showing whether claimed machine usage is conventional or represents a technological improvement. See MPEP §2106.05(a) for improvements to computer functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how particularly the claim confines the judicial exception: broad applicability across many fields or claiming every mode of achieving an effect suggests merely adding 'apply it'; limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad, result-oriented recitations that do not restrict how the effect is achieved are likely not meaningful limitations (cites Internet Patents Corp., O’Reilly v. Morse, The Telephone Cases). In contrast, combinations that specify how interactions are manipulated to yield a desired result (DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Diehr) can be meaningful. Consider whether limitations integrate the exception into a technical process or are mere field-of-use token additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. 'Extra-solution activity' are activities incidental to the primary process/product (pre-solution or post-solution) that are nominal or tangential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pre-solution (gathering data), post-solution (printer output). Addition of insignificant extra-solution activity — especially if well-understood or conventional — does not amount to an inventive concept (cites Parker v. Flook, Mayo). Examiners should evaluate each claim on its own merits and consider other Step 2B factors (particular machine, particular transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field-of-use/tech environment) when determining insignificance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the extra-solution limitation is well-known or conventional, which supports a finding that it is token or insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases finding well-known limitations to be token include Bilski (well-known random analysis techniques), Flook, and Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem. Co. (use of a well-known XML tag). If a limitation is known in the field, explain why it does or does not meaningfully limit the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the limitation imposes meaningful limits on the claim such that it is not nominally or tangentially related to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that are merely incidental or token (e.g., restricting public access to media, minor menu features) have been held insignificant (cites Ultramercial, Apple v. Ameranth). Show how the limitation materially confines claim scope rather than being a nominal addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the limitation merely amounts to necessary data gathering or outputting (i.e., uses of the judicial exception that are required for any use are likely insignificant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data gathering or presenting results (e.g., measuring metabolites in Mayo; presenting offers and gathering statistics in OIP Technologies) are often insignificant. Explain whether the recited data activities are intrinsic to every use of the exception or instead are integrated inventive steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of mere data gathering considered insignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found the following to be mere data gathering and therefore insignificant extra-solution activity: performing clinical tests to obtain inputs, testing a system for response, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transaction information via the Internet to verify credit card transactions, consulting/updating an activity log, determining biomarker levels in blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples (In re Grams; In re Meyers; OIP Technologies; CyberSource; Ultramercial; Mayo) as analogous guidance when evaluating claimed data-gathering steps; explain claim-specific parallels or distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of selecting particular data sources or types considered insignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a particular data source or limiting the type of data (e.g., limiting a database index to XML tags, taking only table-based food orders, selecting information types in a power-grid environment, requiring a request to view an advertisement) has been treated as insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases include Intellectual Ventures I v. Erie Indem. Co., Ameranth, Electric Power Group v. Alstom, Ultramercial. Explain whether such selection steps are merely narrowing by data source/type without adding inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of insignificant application (post-solution or trivial physical steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have described steps such as cutting hair after determining style or printing/downloading generated menus as insignificant application of an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Brown and Ameranth for non-precedential examples; explain whether post-solution physical steps are integrated or merely incidental to the claimed inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant computer implementation as extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation (using generic computer functionality) as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity or as a mere instruction to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Fort Properties v. American Master Lease, Bancorp Services v. Sun Life, and cross-reference MPEP §2106.05(f) for additional guidance about insignificant computer implementation. Distinguish claims that improve computer functionality (Enfish, McRO) from those that merely use generic computer functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must explain when added elements are insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete reasoning (e.g., adding a final storing step to a mathematical formula does not add a meaningful limitation). See MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating eligibility rejections and consider particular machine, transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, and field-of-use factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use and technological environment limitations are not per se inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that merely link a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (i.e., 'field of use' limitations) do not amount to significantly more than the exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit (Parker v. Flook, Bilski, Affinity Labs) hold that token field-of-use restrictions (e.g., limiting use to a particular industry or device type) do not confer eligibility. Compare with Diamond v. Diehr where limitations were integrated into a process. Evaluate whether the limitation is integrated into and alters how the claimed steps are performed, rather than being incidental or token.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into the claim as a whole vs. token field-of-use additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the additional element is integrated into the claim as a whole (meaningfully affects how steps are carried out) rather than merely incidentally limiting the field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrated, specific limitations acting in concert to transform a product/process (Diehr) can make a claim eligible; incidental, token additions (e.g., merely stating a device or audience) do not (Flook, Affinity Labs). Look for changes to the sequence, structure, or functioning caused by the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of limitations described as mere field-of-use/technological-environment additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include limiting drug administration to a specific patient population, identifying participants as commodity providers/consumers, limiting use of a formula to a wheel's circumference, specifying that monitoring audit log data occurs in a computer environment, and restricting virus screening to a telephone network or Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Mayo (drug administration), Bilski (hedging risk participants), Flook (formula limited to wheel), FairWarning v. Iatric Sys. (computer environment), Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (telephone network/Internet). Use these to analogize when field-of-use restrictions are token rather than integrated.
